name: ラーメン二郎 新宿小滝橋通り店 (Ramen Jiro Shinjuku Kotakibashi-dori)

claims.text: Extremely small, single-line open kitchen where noodles, broth, and toppings for every order pass through the same equipment — no separated prep area exists for allergen-sensitive orders.
The tare/soup is described as a soy-sauce (shoyu) based, micro-emulsified broth with a pronounced soy sauce character — standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat.
Broth is a pork-bone (tonkotsu) base simmered with pork, and standard bowls are topped with generous chashu pork and often pork back fat (abura); no plant-based broth or protein option is offered.

name: Sagatani Jūwari Soba, Jimbocho (十割蕎麦 嵯峨谷 神保町店)

claims.text: Tempura and kakiage are deep-fried on-site ('揚げたて'), so a shared fryer and airborne wheat flour (batter/dredge) are present in this small standing shop.
Mitigating factor: the entire shop is 100% buckwheat soba, so noodle boiling water is not shared with wheat udon.
The tsuyu/broth is a standard sweet-savory soy-based soba broth ('甘辛濃いめ'), i.e. ordinary wheat-containing soy sauce, not tamari — the noodle is wheat-free but the sauce as served is not.
Standard tsuyu is bonito (katsuo) dashi, so soba as served is not vegan even though the noodles are plant-based.
Fast, cheap standing-soba shop with ticket-machine ordering; no allergy protocol, allergen menu, or gluten-free claim appears in any source.
Genuine 十割 (100% buckwheat) noodles, stone-milled and made in-house daily — the noodle itself contains no wheat.
All-soba shop means the boiling water is not shared with wheat udon, unlike typical mixed soba/udon stands.

name: 魚料理 のじま (Sakana Ryōri Nojima)

claims.text: The restaurant's signature dish, the wild yellowtail (buri) rice bowl, is dressed in a soy-sauce-and-wasabi marinade (tare), meaning standard wheat-containing shoyu is used in at least this core menu item.
The owner personally selects only fresh, wild-caught (never frozen or farmed) fish each morning at the Toyosu market, and fillets it himself, reflecting decades of fishmonger experience.

name: Salad Cafe 京王百貨店新宿店 (Salad Cafe Keio Department Store Shinjuku)

claims.text: Japanese-style salads and deli sides at Salad Cafe commonly use soy-sauce-based dressings and seasonings, which typically contain wheat; no wheat-free dressing option was confirmed for this location.
Salad Cafe's parent operations state a commitment to providing accurate allergy and nutritional information for its products so customers can make informed choices.

The shop offers a wide daily rotation of 15-18 vegetable-based salads and deli items sold by weight, so diners can visually select and portion exactly what they want rather than ordering a fixed set dish.

name: しゃぶしゃぶ温野菜 浅草店 (Shabu-shabu On'yasai Asakusa-ten (Shabu Shab)

claims.text: The all-you-can-eat shabu-shabu format uses shared pots and cooking/washing equipment across meat and vegetable items, creating cross-contact risk for allergen-sensitive diners.

The chain's signature "Sandaime Kiwami Dashi" broth is built around a white soy sauce blended with sardine, soda-bonito and mackerel stock — soy sauce (and thus wheat) is in the base cooking liquid itself, not only in a side dipping sauce.

The default/signature broths are fish-stock based (sardine, soda-katsuo, mackerel), and even the soy-milk broth option is cut with bonito and kombu dashi, so no broth on the standard menu is confirmed vegan; the restaurant's core product is all-you-can-eat meat shabu-shabu.
Staff can reportedly provide a printed 7-major-allergen reference sheet on request, but the chain notes shared cooking/washing equipment means cross-contamination cannot be ruled out.

The chain is built around a large, frequently-rotating selection of domestic (国産) vegetables served alongside meat in an all-you-can-eat format, with several distinct proprietary broths to choose from.

name: 渋谷西村フルーツパーラー 道玄坂店 (Shibuya Nishimura Fruit Parlor Dogenzaka)

claims.text: No dedicated gluten-free preparation area or process was documented; wheat-containing bread and cake components are used throughout the parfait and sandwich menu.
Dairy whipped cream and ice cream are core components of virtually every parfait and fruit sandwich, with no vegan cream substitute identified.
Menu listings note allergens per dish (e.g. 乳・小麦・卵・アーモンド — dairy, wheat, egg, almond), but no specific gluten-free or vegan accommodation protocol beyond standard allergen labeling was found.
Fresh, high-quality seasonal fruit is the centerpiece of every dish, giving naturally gluten-free and plant-based components (the fruit itself) even though prepared dishes are not GF/vegan overall.

name: シズラー 新宿三井ビル店 (Sizzler Shinjuku Mitsui Building)

claims.text: The self-serve Premium Salad Bar places wheat-containing items — bread, pasta, and taco tortillas — on the same buffet line as the fresh vegetables and fruit, using shared serving utensils, so cross-contact is likely for anyone strictly avoiding gluten.

Sizzler is a chain which typically means a high risk of cross-contact, and it is likely not possible to dine safely at this establishment if you have celiac disease or must avoid cross-contact; the Shinjuku Mitsui location is NOT a dedicated gluten-free facility and may not be safe for those with celiac disease.

The Premium Salad Bar offers 70+ items always available including seasonal vegetables, fresh deli salads, soup, fruit, pasta, tacos, dessert and drinks — all set out on the same self-serve bar, i.e., wheat items (pasta, tacos/tortillas, bread) physically alongside produce.

EU/US 'gluten-free labeling' and Japan's 'allergy labeling' are based on different standards; gluten-free does not necessarily mean wheat-free — Japan has no unified gluten-free standard, so an allergen menu does not equal celiac-safe handling.

Salad bar dressings are numerous (5 dressings, 6 vinegars, 3 oils, plus mayonnaise) and not itemized for allergens at the bar; Japanese buffet soups/dressings commonly rely on bonito dashi and contain dairy/egg — relevant to hidden animal products for vegans and unlabeled gluten sources.

With 70+ items including whole fresh seasonal vegetables and fruit, the salad bar gives diners plenty of naturally plant-based, unprocessed options to build a meal around without relying on prepared or sauced dishes.

name: シズラー新宿東宝ビル店 (Sizzler Shinjuku Toho Building)

claims.text: The salad bar is a shared self-serve buffet where guests use common serving utensils across all dishes, so cross-contact between gluten-containing and gluten-free items is possible even though many items are naturally gluten-free.

Sizzler Shinjuku Mitsui Building (a different, nearby branch) is described as 'not a dedicated gluten-free facility and may not be safe for those with celiac disease' — no branch has celiac-grade confirmation, including this one.

Chain-level assessment: 'As a chain restaurant, Sizzler typically means a high risk of cross-contact, and it is likely not possible to dine safely at this establishment if you have celiac disease or must avoid cross-contact.' A manager reportedly said only 'a couple of items in the salad bar' are gluten-free and those are 'subject to cross contamination,' and reviewers 'wouldn't trust the salad because of so much cross contamination.'

Salad-bar croutons are wheat-flour bread fried in oil; unpackaged buffet dishes carry no labeling obligation and even trace exposure can trigger symptoms, so wheat-allergic/celiac diners must confirm cross-contamination directly with staff — i.e. the buffet is a documented cross-contact hazard, not a safe self-serve GF environment.

The Toho Building branch opened in early June 2025 (JR Shinjuku ~5 min); searches for branch-specific allergen/wheat/vegan/dashi accommodation returned no confirmation of GF handling or vegan prep for this location.

Soups, curries, and dressings on the buffet may contain dashi, meat stock, or dairy, and are served from the same buffet line as vegetable dishes, so strict vegans should check ingredients item by item rather than assume the whole bar is plant-based.

General reporting on the Sizzler Japan chain describes staff providing an allergen-removal menu and a list covering 25+ designated allergen items on request, though this describes chain-wide practice rather than a confirmation specific to the Shinjuku Toho Building branch.

A Tripadvisor review of a different Tokyo Sizzler branch (Setagaya) reported staff bringing an allergy-information folder when asked, suggesting this is a chain-standard practice, though not independently confirmed for this Shinjuku location.

The salad bar is described as offering 70+ items of fresh seasonal vegetables, fruit, and made-to-order components, giving diners with dietary restrictions substantial control over what goes on their own plate.
